sweep_summary: Two title-hits for Fijian. (1) Milner 1989 (Henderson festschrift, pp. 59-88) was obtained in full from the SEAlang SALA archive (image scan, scanned at 200 dpi, 30 pp.): 'prosodic' there is Firthian and the paper is about the consonant of transitive suffixes and its association with base consonants/vowels; it never mentions accent or stress, so it is silent on the catalog's classification and needs no acquisition. (2) Schütz 1999 'Fijian Accent' (OL 38(1):139-151, DOI 10.2307/3623396) is the one genuinely relevant item: a dedicated accent article by the author of the deciding source, but closed on JSTOR with no OA location per Unpaywall and OpenAlex and no abstract in any record; not read, priority high (Harvard has online access via the Harvard library catalogue). Bonus first-hand statement read: Schütz & Komaitai 1971 Spoken Fijian p. xxxii (open on UH ScholarSpace, scanned) — stress on long vowels, else penult unless final vowel is long, plus initial secondary stress in four-syllable words — which confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding but does not supersede Schütz 1985. lookups were done by direct download of Crossref, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Glottolog, HathiTrust, Open Library, ScholarSpace and SEAlang.

new_statements.quote: Stress. In any series of syllables, some are pronounced with more loudness, or stress, than others. In some cases, the stress is predictable. It will occur under the following conditions: 1. On long vowels. 2. On the second-to-last vowel, unless the last vowel is long. 3. In four-syllable words, on not only the second-to-last syllable, but also the first. For longer words, only conditions 1 and 2 hold. Other stresses are unpredictable. [p. xxxii] ...The difference between i and ī is that the latter lasts longer than the former and always receives stress. [pp. xxxi-xxxii]

Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press. Open-access edition on UH ScholarSpace, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, handle 10125/63324.
new_statements.locator: Introduction, section 'Stress', p. xxxii (pdf page 33); preceding 'Long vowels' paragraph pp. xxxi-xxxii
new_statements.reading: Stress falls on every long vowel; otherwise on the penultimate vowel, unless the final vowel is long (in which case the final long vowel takes it); four-syllable words carry an additional (secondary) stress on the first syllable. This is a weight-sensitive final-long-else-penult system with long vowels as the heavy syllables, i.e. the same rule the catalog codes as 'weight' from Schütz 1985; the 1971 text uses 'stress' and a word domain rather than the 1985 'accent'/'measure' framing. Not a works with stress in the title (found while checking ScholarSpace for open Schütz works) and not superior to the 1985 grammar: it is an earlier pedagogical statement by the same author.

sources.citation: Wolff, John U. (2003). Fijian reflexes of the Proto Austronesian phonemes. In Issues in Austronesian historical phonology. pp. 209-227.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Stress in Fijian falls on the penult of the phonological word. That is, if the root is unsuffixed, the stress falls on the penult of the root, but if the root is suffixed, the stress moves away from the penult - to the final syllable of the root if the suffix has one syllable.
sources.locator: printed p. 214, footnote 7; also p. 211 §2.2: 'Fijian words which are not atonic (i.e. those that are not stressless) have a minimum of two morae; that is, the…
sources.note: Historical-phonology paper (PAn > Fijian reflexes); stress is treated only as background in footnotes. States penultimate stress on the phonological word (root + suffix), a two-mora minimum for non-clitic words with long vowels counting two morae, and that stressed vs unstressed position conditions vowel reflexes (*aw > /au/ under stress, /o/ unstressed; unstressed *u elided in the antepenult). No mention of weight-sensitivity (long vowels or diphthongs attracting stress), secondary stress, or tone; the catalog's weight rule is neither confirmed nor contradicted. Uncited stress statement; Gera

sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: 2.4 Stress. The units of distribution for stress placement are the group and the contour span (or tone group). A group consists of a sequence of two or three syllables in which the penultimate syllable is stressed. A group is often, but not always a single morpheme. In the sequence navosavakanabukelevumakawadjina 'the old Nabukelevu language' the groups are navosa + vaka + nabuke + levu + makawa + djina. [...] Group stress is predictable if group boundaries are marked. As such boundaries are not completely determinable on grammatical grounds it is necessary to posit a junctural phoneme /+/ between groups. The less satisfactory alternative is to treat stress as unpredictable, i.e. as phonemic. Some grammatical morphemes appear to be inherently unstressed, but this matter has not been systematically studied. A contour span consists of one or more groups spoken as a single fluent unit, carrying a continuous intonation contour which contains at least one contour stress or peak, falling on a single syllable. This intonation peak often falls on the penultimate syllable of the span. [Section 2.3, same page:] Syllable shapes are V (vowel) and CV (consonant+vowel). A long vowel, V-macron, i

sources.quote: Main stress falls on a heavy final syllable, or if absent, the penult. Then, additional stress is placed on all heavy syllables and on every other light syllable counting leftwards from the previous stress. This means that a heavy resets the count for iteration of stress

sources.citation: Milner, G.B. 1989. On prosodic relations between Fijian bases and verbal suffixes. In Jeremy H.C.S. Davidson (ed.), South-east Asian Linguistics: Essays in Honour of Eugénie J.A. Henderson, 59-88. London: School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London.
sources.quote: Arms, following Krupa, uses the term 'dissociative'; Hockett speaks of 'dissimilative tendencies', while I have spoken in this article of 'phonotactic constraints' and of 'prosodic constraint'. The preferential association of certain suffixes with certain vowels in the base which is discussed here is the opposite of a constraint. Hence the title of the article which attempts to subsume both phenomena under the term 'prosodic' in the sense first used by J.R. Firth and the London school of linguists with which he is associated (cf. Firth 1948). [p. 83, n. 31]
sources.locator: whole chapter (30 pp.); definition of 'prosodic' in note 31, p. 83; vowel-length remark p. 78
sources.note: Nothing. 'Prosodic' is used in the Firthian sense: the paper is about which consonant (-ca, -ga, -ka, -ma, -na, -ra, -ta, -va..) a Fijian transitive suffix takes and how that choice is constrained by / associated with the consonants and vowels of the base (dissimilation, place of articulation, C+V associations), with historical comparison to Indonesian stem-final consonants. The 30 scanned pages contain zero occurrences of 'accent' or 'stress'; the only length remark (p. 78) is that the orthography 'does not take vowel length into account. Since the latter is phonemic, it is a serious defect'…
sources.venue: South-east Asian Linguisitics: Essays in Honour of Eugénie J.A.

tone.quote: Despite some preliminary insights into its prosodic structure, systematic studies on focus marking mechanisms in Fijian are lacking. As mentioned in Schütz (1985), while the phrase peak, or phonological accent, typically occurs at the end of a sentence, it can shift when expressing a contrastive situation.
